opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think "The Bitter Lesson" is one of those essays that's easy to quote and hard to really absorb.

The core idea, as I understand it, is that over the long run, methods that can take advantage of more computation, like search and learning, tend to beat methods where we carefully encode human knowledge. Researchers keep wanting to build in our own understanding of how vision or language or chess works, because it feels smart and it gives quick wins. But eventually a more general approach, given enough data and compute, overtakes it. That's the "bitter" part. The clever things we were proud of turn out not to matter that much.

I saw this firsthand. When I was working on Caffe around 2013, computer vision was full of hand-engineered features: SIFT, HOG, all kinds of carefully designed pipelines. Then convolutional networks trained on GPUs with ImageNet-scale data came along, and within a couple of years most of that engineering was gone. The network learned better features than we could design. That was a very concrete version of Sutton's point.

That said, I don't read the lesson as "just add more GPUs and stop thinking." Two things are often overlooked.

First, scale is a systems problem. To actually benefit from general methods, someone has to make computation usable: frameworks, compilers, distributed training, efficient inference, reliable infrastructure. Much of the progress we credit to "scale" is really progress in engineering that made scale affordable and practical. That's a big part of why I've spent my career on the infrastructure side.

Second, the choice of which general method to scale still matters a lot. Transformers, self-supervised pretraining, the right objective functions: these are human insights, but they're insights about how to let the model learn, not about what it should know. I think that's the healthy reading of Sutton. Put your intelligence into the learning mechanism and the system, not into hard-coding the answer.

And there's a practical, economic side too. Compute isn't free. In industry you have to ask what the cost per token or per query is, and whether the capability gain justifies it. So the lesson for me is: bet on methods that get better with scale, and then work very hard to make that scale efficient. Those two go together.

r001.rationale: It says methods that exploit more computation, such as search and learning, tend to beat methods that encode human knowledge.

r002.rationale: It describes general approaches overtaking hand-designed methods given enough data and compute, and cites ImageNet-scale data as an example.

r003.rationale: It says convolutional networks learned better features than hand-engineered pipelines, but does not identify those as simpler statistical patterns discovered from large-scale data and computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I read Sutton's "Bitter Lesson" is actually pretty personal, because I lived through the transition he's describing.

When I was building Caffe around 2013, 2014, the field was still full of what Sutton would call hand-crafted knowledge. People spent years designing features like SIFT and HOG, and the model was almost an afterthought. Then AlexNet came along, and the thing that made the difference wasn't a clever new insight about vision. It was that someone finally had enough compute and enough data to let a fairly general method, convolution plus gradient descent, learn the features itself. All that careful human engineering got washed away in a couple of years. That was a bitter pill for a lot of smart people.

So the core of the lesson, as I understand it, is this: methods that scale with computation eventually beat methods that encode human priors, because compute keeps getting cheaper and human cleverness doesn't. Search and learning are the two general-purpose mechanisms that benefit from more compute, and over the long run they win. We saw it in chess, in Go, in vision, in speech, and now very obviously in language models.

But I want to add two caveats from the engineering side, because I think people sometimes read Sutton as "just throw more GPUs at it," and that's not quite right.

First, "general methods" still require enormous amounts of human work. It's just a different kind of work. Instead of designing features, you're designing infrastructure. You're figuring out how to shard a model across thousands of chips, how to keep utilization high, how to build data pipelines that don't fall over. The lesson moves human effort from the algorithm to the system. When I was at Facebook and later at Alibaba, most of our time went to making scale actually work, not to coming up with new architectures.

Second, scale is a direction, not a destination. Every generation, someone says we've hit the wall, and then a more general method shows up that uses the compute better. Transformers used compute better than LSTMs. Mixture of experts uses it better than dense models in some regimes. So the question I ask myself is never "is scale enough?" It's "what's the simplest method that can absorb the next ten times more compute without breaking?" That framing has been very reliable for me.

The last thing I'd say is that the lesson is humbling in a healthy way. Researchers want to feel that their insight is the thing that mattered. Sutton is telling us that often the insight is just a stepping stone, and the real driver is making it easy for a general method to learn from more data. If you accept that, you build differently. You optimize for flexibility and throughput rather than for elegance. That's a less romantic view of AI, but it's the one that has kept being right.

r001.rationale: The response says methods that scale with computation eventually beat methods built around human priors, and describes general methods benefiting from more compute.

r002.rationale: It explicitly connects the lesson to having enough data as well as compute, saying both let a general method learn features.

r003.rationale: It says learned features displaced manually designed features, but does not clearly characterize the learned patterns as simpler statistical patterns discovered through large-scale computation and data.

astra-6.text:
I think Sutton’s “bitter lesson” is that, over the long run, general methods that can take advantage of more computation tend to outperform approaches built around human knowledge of a particular problem.

The temptation for researchers is to say, “I understand this task, so let me encode that understanding into the system.” And that can produce a very good result in the short term. But it can also put a ceiling on the system. A more general learning or search method may initially look less efficient, yet keep improving as you give it more compute and data.

I wouldn’t interpret that as saying research doesn’t matter, or that you should just make everything bigger. The research question becomes: are we designing a method that can actually benefit from scale? You still need the right algorithms and the systems to run them efficiently.

To me, the lesson is about where we put our intelligence as researchers: into building mechanisms that can learn, rather than trying to specify everything they should know.

r001.rationale: It says general methods that take advantage of more computation tend to outperform approaches built around human knowledge of a particular problem.

r002.rationale: It describes methods improving as they receive more compute and data, identifying data as part of the scaling lesson.

r003.rationale: It contrasts general learning or search methods with encoded human knowledge, but does not state that simpler statistical patterns found through scale outperform manually designed features.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Sutton’s point is that, over time, methods that can take advantage of more computation tend to win over methods that depend on us encoding a lot of human knowledge. We often try to make a system smarter by giving it the structure we think it should have. That can help in the short term, but it can also put a ceiling on what the system can learn.

The lesson isn’t simply “make everything bigger.” It’s to choose methods that keep improving as you give them more compute and more experience. Search and learning are powerful because they let the machine discover solutions instead of requiring us to specify those solutions in advance.

That changes where we put our engineering effort. Rather than handcrafting every piece of intelligence, we build the infrastructure and learning process that make experimentation at scale possible. There’s still a lot of human ingenuity involved—it goes into creating a system that can learn beyond what we already know.

r001.rationale: It says methods that benefit from more computation tend to win over methods built around extensive human knowledge, and favors methods that improve with more compute.

r002.rationale: It mentions more experience, but does not clearly identify large amounts of data as part of the lesson.

r003.rationale: It contrasts learning and search with handcrafting solutions, but does not state that simpler statistical patterns found through large-scale computation and data may outperform manually designed features.
